paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers learning from labeled source data to target data without target labels. Many approaches compare source and target samples in a learned feature space and try to reduce their statistical differences. This paper instead organizes adaptation around class prototypes: representations that summarize individual classes and provide reference points for target features.

The proposed probabilistic framework extracts these prototypes and aligns target features with them. The motivation is to avoid difficulties associated with direct sample comparisons, including sampling variability, unequal class frequencies, and concerns about access to private source data. Prototypes make class summaries central to adaptation while keeping memory and computation requirements manageable.

The authors demonstrate the approach across single-source and multiple-source adaptation, class imbalance, and settings involving private source data. It introduces no additional model parameters and adds a moderate amount of computation beyond the source model. Its reported performance is competitive with leading methods, supporting prototypes as a practical basis for adaptation across these different settings.
neurips-2021-a-prototype-oriented-framew.tldr: A probabilistic adaptation framework aligns target features with class prototypes, achieving competitive results with no additional model parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to build accurate ensemble predictors when training information comes from several source domains. Boosting combines predictors into a stronger ensemble, but the authors show that standard convex combinations cannot generally solve this multiple-source problem. The result identifies a limitation of the combination rule itself, making that rule an important part of the learning problem.

The proposed algorithm, MULTIBOOST, uses a domain-weighted combination instead. This changes how the ensemble brings together information from different sources. The authors analyze the algorithm and establish favorable theoretical guarantees, giving the approach a formal basis alongside its practical evaluation. The central contribution is therefore both a different combination strategy and a boosting procedure designed around it.

Experiments on text, image, and tabular data show MULTIBOOST outperforming natural comparison methods. The paper also extends the approach to federated learning and reports favorable results there. A separate multiclass extension, MCMULTIBOOST, receives an experimental evaluation as well, broadening the range of prediction settings addressed by the framework.
neurips-2021-boosting-with-multiple-sour.tldr: MULTIBOOST uses domain-weighted ensembles to learn from multiple sources, with theoretical guarantees and favorable empirical results.

paragraphs: Adding mistakes to training labels seems counterproductive, but this paper asks when deliberately increasing label noise can help. Its focus is uneven noise: some groups of examples have less reliable labels than others. Increasing noise in a cleaner group can balance these rates, potentially making learning easier and improving fairness guarantees against label bias.

The authors quantify the trade-off between losing label information and reducing the difficulty of the learning problem. Their analysis identifies circumstances in which balancing through additional noise benefits generalization or fairness. The claim is conditional: the value comes from an appropriate change in the pattern of noise, rather than from adding arbitrary errors to labels.

The resulting method supports learning with noisy labels both with and without a fairness constraint. A key obstacle is that clean ground-truth labels are unavailable, and the noisier group is unknown. The paper proposes a detector that indicates which group may have higher noise without those clean labels, establishes the solution's effectiveness formally, and supports it experimentally.
neurips-2021-can-less-be-more-when-incre.tldr: Under identified conditions, deliberately balancing unequal label-noise rates can improve generalization or fairness despite reducing label information.

paragraphs: Many causal inference methods are developed for independent observations, while event-stream data consist of repeated occurrences at irregular times. Different event types share a timeline and need not happen together. This paper develops a framework for asking causal questions between pairs of event variables in that setting, using multivariate point processes to represent the streams.

The approach extends Rubin's treatment-effect framework, including average treatment effects and propensity scores, to these temporal data. A point process takes the representational role that a joint probability distribution plays for independent observations. This allows the proposed causal quantity to be formulated around asynchronous, recurrent events rather than treating the data as ordinary independent records.

The authors theoretically justify the framework and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of their proposed measure. They also evaluate it using synthetic and real-world event datasets. In these experiments, it performs better than the tested pairwise causal association scores, supporting the usefulness of a causal formulation built specifically for event streams.
neurips-2021-causal-inference-for-event-.tldr: The paper extends treatment-effect estimation to irregular recurrent event streams and demonstrates advantages over tested pairwise causal association scores.

paragraphs: Clustering incomplete data is difficult because each point may have a different set of observed coordinates. Distances and clustering costs are evaluated only where values are available, so the information used varies from point to point. This paper constructs coresets for data with multiple missing coordinates, extending earlier constructions that allowed only one.

A coreset is a small proxy dataset, typically a weighted subset, that approximately preserves the clustering objective for every possible choice of centers. The authors provide such constructions for both k-means and k-median. Their size depends on accuracy, dimension, dataset size, the number of clusters, and the maximum number of missing coordinates per point.

The importance-sampling construction runs in near-linear time. It also turns an existing quadratic-time approximation scheme for k-means with missing values into a near-linear-time method. On real datasets, the coresets offer a size-versus-accuracy trade-off, generally beat uniform sampling, and substantially accelerate a Lloyd-style clustering heuristic. These results connect the formal approximation guarantee with practical computational savings.
neurips-2021-coresets-for-clustering-wit.tldr: Small weighted summaries preserve clustering costs for data with multiple missing coordinates and enable faster clustering.

paragraphs: This paper learns dense keypoints using a semi-supervised framework that draws on unlabeled images from multiple viewpoints. The central difficulty is finding exact matches between dense keypoints across views. The inverse keypoint mapping cannot be analytically derived or differentiated, preventing straightforward use of multiview supervision methods that depend on exact correspondences.

The authors replace that requirement with a probabilistic epipolar constraint. A matchability score expresses how likely points are to correspond, and these scores weight geometric errors across possible matches. The resulting constraint operates over whole correspondence fields while requiring collective geometric consistency. This provides a training signal even when an individual point's exact match is unavailable.

A twin-network architecture builds affinity matrices to minimize these probabilistic errors across view pairs. Distillation from a pretrained model provides regularization intended to prevent degenerate solutions. The reported comparisons show improvements in keypoint accuracy, consistency across views, and 3D reconstruction accuracy, including over non-differentiable bootstrapping. Together, the results support soft geometric correspondence as useful supervision for dense detection.
neurips-2021-dense-keypoints-via-multivi.tldr: Probabilistic geometric matching enables dense keypoint learning from unlabeled multiview images without requiring exact point correspondences.

paragraphs: Federated learning with user-level differential privacy limits how much each user's model update can contribute. A common mechanism clips updates to a fixed maximum norm. Choosing that threshold beforehand is difficult because update sizes depend on the model, loss, data available on devices, learning rate, and other training choices.

This paper replaces the fixed threshold with an adaptive value drawn from a chosen quantile of the update-norm distribution. The quantile is estimated during training using differential privacy, so adaptation itself is included in the privacy accounting. The authors report that the estimate tracks the desired quantile closely while consuming a negligible amount of the privacy budget.

The method is compatible with compression and secure aggregation, and its privacy analysis can be combined directly with DP Federated Averaging. Experiments find that clipping at the median update norm works well across a range of federated tasks. In those evaluations, this removes the need to tune a clipping hyperparameter, simplifying an otherwise task-dependent part of private training.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-lear.tldr: Privately tracking a quantile of user-update sizes provides an adaptive clipping threshold that works well across tested federated learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the difficulty of understanding how a deep neural network reaches a decision. It introduces VOTEN, an explainable network built around hierarchical voting between explicitly represented latent concepts. The aim is to make the decision process visible through the model's own structure while retaining the ability to fit complex data.

VOTEN uses expressive single-valued voting functions to connect these concepts. This makes the functions between concepts central to both prediction and explanation, rather than relying on large combinations of features. The authors theoretically analyze its main components and establish relationships and advantages relative to a multilayer perceptron, the basic architecture underlying many neural networks.

The paper also develops efficient algorithms that explicitly display VOTEN's decision process, making the architecture more usable as an explanatory model. Experiments across multiple real-world datasets support its predictive performance and explainability. The contribution combines an architecture designed for interpretable decisions, a theoretical comparison with a familiar network structure, and empirical evidence about its behavior.
neurips-2021-discerning-decision-making-.tldr: VOTEN models decisions as hierarchical votes between latent concepts, combining predictive fitting with explicit decision-process explanations.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples use carefully chosen perturbations to alter a model's prediction. This paper investigates them through the distinction between robust and non-robust features, which earlier work has argued is a primary cause of adversarial behavior. Its contribution is a method for explicitly separating a learned representation into these two kinds of feature units.

The method uses the Information Bottleneck perspective to examine information flow through the representation. It injects noise variation into individual feature units and uses the magnitude of that variation to classify units as robust or non-robust. This turns the conceptual distinction into an operational procedure for inspecting features inside a model.

Experiments show that the separated features are strongly correlated with adversarial predictions and contain semantic information people can perceive. The authors also construct an attack that intensifies gradients associated with prediction-relevant non-robust features and demonstrate its effectiveness at breaking robustness. The findings connect the feature separation to both interpretable content and a concrete mechanism for adversarial manipulation.
neurips-2021-distilling-robust-and-non-r.tldr: An Information Bottleneck method separates robust and non-robust features and uses the latter to construct effective adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a label to every image pixel, but convolutional encoders often reduce spatial resolution substantially. A decoder must recover detailed predictions from that compressed output. This paper proposes a dynamic neural representational decoder, or NRD, that represents local patches of semantic labels using compact neural networks.

Each encoder-output location corresponds to a local label patch. NRD dynamically generates a neural representation for that patch, conditioned on the encoder's output, and decodes the desired labels from it. This design exploits an assumed smoothness in semantic label space, allowing local structure to be represented compactly while producing high-resolution segmentation predictions.

The empirical results connect this representation choice to computational savings. NRD can outperform the DeeplabV3+ decoder at approximately 30% of its computational complexity. It also achieves competitive performance against methods using dilated encoders at approximately 15% of their computation. Experiments on Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context support both its effectiveness and efficiency across the evaluated segmentation datasets.
neurips-2021-dynamic-neural-representati.tldr: Dynamically generated compact networks decode local label patches into high-resolution segmentations with substantially lower computation in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: A model's overall performance can conceal poor results for particular parts of a population. This paper evaluates the worst performance among all subpopulations of a specified size, with membership defined through selected core attributes. Those attributes can be continuous, and the formulation accommodates complex intersections of characteristics in disadvantaged groups.

The authors develop a scalable two-stage estimation procedure for this robustness measure. Estimating model performance conditional on the attributes is central to its accuracy. The procedure comes with finite-sample convergence guarantees, including dimension-free convergence results. The influence of attribute dimension enters through the out-of-sample error of the conditional-performance estimate, rather than a direct complexity penalty based on that dimension.

This distinction matters because it ties evaluation accuracy to how well the relevant performance pattern can actually be learned. On real datasets, the authors demonstrate robustness certification and identification of unreliable models before deployment. These findings concern the defined family of attribute-based subpopulations and provide a more targeted assessment than an aggregate score over the whole population.
neurips-2021-evaluating-model-performanc.tldr: A two-stage estimator assesses worst-case performance across attribute-defined subpopulations, with finite-sample guarantees and practical robustness evaluations.

paragraphs: Continual learning must handle successive tasks while balancing generalization against catastrophic forgetting. This paper gives that tension a formal structure using dynamic programming and a two-player sequential game. The formulation makes the competing costs explicit, providing a mathematical way to reason about how they can be balanced during learning.

The first player maximizes the cost associated with a lack of generalization, while the second minimizes the cost associated with forgetting. Within this formulation, the authors prove that a balance point exists for each task. They also establish stability: once the players reach that point, they remain there. This is a statement about the balance in the proposed game.

The paper then introduces balanced continual learning, or BCL, an algorithm designed to attain that balance. Empirical comparisons show BCL matching or exceeding the performance of leading methods. The theoretical and experimental contributions play complementary roles: the game establishes a stable balancing target, while the experiments support the usefulness of an algorithm designed around it.
neurips-2021-formalizing-the-generalizat.tldr: A two-player formulation establishes a stable balance between generalization and forgetting and motivates the empirically competitive BCL algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper introduces invertible Dense Networks, called i-DenseNets, as a more parameter-efficient extension of Residual Flows. The architectural challenge is to use concatenated representations while preserving invertibility. The authors address it by analyzing the Lipschitz continuity of concatenation and enforcing the Lipschitz condition required by their construction.

Two additions improve the resulting architecture. Learnable weighted concatenation lets the network adjust the contributions of the representations it combines, while also indicating their importance through the learned weights. A new activation function, Concatenated LipSwish, is designed with an enforceable Lipschitz condition. These components connect architectural flexibility to the mathematical constraints used to maintain invertibility.

At an equal parameter budget, i-DenseNet outperforms Residual Flow and other evaluated flow-based models on density estimation measured in bits per dimension. It also outperforms Residual Flows in a hybrid setting that combines generative and discriminative modeling. The findings support the proposed construction as a way to improve performance while controlling model size and retaining the required invertible structure.
neurips-2021-invertible-densenets-with-c.tldr: i-DenseNets combine Lipschitz-controlled concatenation and a new activation to improve invertible-model performance at an equal parameter budget.

paragraphs: This paper studies safe exploration in episodic constrained reinforcement learning. Earlier results allowed both reward regret and constraint violation to grow roughly with the square root of the number of episodes, ignoring logarithmic factors. The authors ask whether violations can be kept smaller while preserving favorable learning behavior.

When a strictly safe policy is already known, their algorithm achieves zero constraint violation with arbitrarily high probability while retaining the square-root order of reward regret. It combines optimism and pessimism in its treatment of uncertainty. This allows exploration for reward while accounting conservatively for the constraints that define safety.

The paper also considers a weaker starting point: a strictly safe policy is known to exist, but the learner does not know which policy it is. Here, a primal-dual algorithm with optimistic primal estimates and pessimistic dual updates achieves bounded constraint violation with arbitrarily high probability. The distinction between these results is essential: knowing a safe policy supports the stronger zero-violation guarantee.
neurips-2021-learning-policies-with-zero.tldr: A known strictly safe policy enables high-probability zero-violation learning, while knowing only that one exists enables bounded violation.

paragraphs: Human-object interaction detection requires locating people and objects and identifying the interactions between them. This paper examines weaknesses in two common approaches. Conventional two-stage systems struggle to position positively interacting human-object pairs, while one-stage systems face difficulty balancing object detection and interaction classification within a multitask learning setup.

The authors propose a one-stage framework that separates these responsibilities through a cascade. Starting from a transformer-based HOI detector, they remove the interaction-classification head to create a human-object pair generator. A relatively isolated classifier then assigns interactions to the generated pairs. Two cascaded decoders can consequently specialize in detection and interaction classification.

This design aims to preserve useful aspects of both families while reducing the competition between their component tasks. The reported evaluation shows a substantial improvement over existing methods, including a 9.32% relative gain in mean average precision on HICO-Det. That result supports task separation within the proposed cascade as an effective architectural choice for the evaluated HOI detection setting.
neurips-2021-mining-the-benefits-of-two-.tldr: Cascaded decoders separate human-object pair detection from interaction classification, delivering a reported 9.32% relative mAP gain on HICO-Det.

paragraphs: Sets create an unusual learning problem because their elements have no fixed order and their size can vary. This paper develops a unified mathematical framework for understanding which functions PointNet, DeepSets, and related architectures can approximate. Hausdorff and Wasserstein metrics play a central role in describing the relevant notions of similarity between inputs.

The authors establish universality results that do not depend on fixing set size. They show that PointNet generally cannot approximate averages of continuous functions over sets, including quantities such as center of mass. For constant-size sets, their results imply that DeepSets is strictly more expressive. Explicit error lower bounds and a construction of arbitrarily many failure examples make this limitation concrete.

A further result concerns sets of unbounded size: any function uniformly approximable by both PointNet and normalized DeepSets must be constant. The paper also proves Lipschitz properties that clarify the architectures' inductive biases. Together, these results show how pooling choices and assumptions about set size determine representational capabilities.
neurips-2021-on-the-representation-power.tldr: The paper characterizes set-network expressiveness, exposing precise differences between PointNet and DeepSets across fixed and unbounded set sizes.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular properties with few labeled examples requires making good use of relationships between molecules. This paper argues that those relationships, and the molecular substructures that matter, change with the property being predicted. Property-Aware Relation networks, or PAR, therefore adapt both molecular representations and their relationships to the target property.

A property-aware embedding function first transforms generic molecular representations into a space emphasizing relevant substructures. An adaptive graph module then jointly estimates relationships among molecules and refines their embeddings. This graph allows the limited label information to propagate among molecules considered similar for the particular property, making the definition of similarity part of the learned solution.

PAR uses meta-learning with selective parameter updates within tasks to separate generic knowledge from property-specific knowledge. On benchmark molecular property datasets, it consistently outperforms the methods included in the evaluation. The experiments also support its ability to learn property-aware embeddings and appropriate relation graphs, connecting the predictive improvements to the intended adaptation of molecular structure and similarity.
neurips-2021-property-aware-relation-net.tldr: PAR adapts molecular embeddings and relation graphs to each target property, improving prediction from limited labeled examples.

paragraphs: Enforcing invariance means requiring a model to give the same result under specified transformations of its input. This paper provides a rigorous generalization benefit for doing so in kernel ridge regression. Its key condition is that the target function itself is invariant under the action of a compact group of transformations.

The authors study invariance imposed through feature averaging and derive a strictly nonzero benefit under their analyzed setting. They identify an effective dimension that governs generalization and depends jointly on the kernel and the transformation group. This ties the benefit to the interaction between the chosen representation and the symmetry being enforced.

The analysis also shows that the group action induces an orthogonal decomposition of both the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and its kernel. This supplies mathematical structure for understanding the effect of invariance on the learned function space. The contribution is a conditional theoretical justification for symmetry-aware kernel learning, with the target's invariance central to the stated result.
neurips-2021-provably-strict-generalisat.tldr: For compact-group-invariant targets, the paper proves a strictly nonzero generalization benefit from enforcing invariance in kernel ridge regression.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning often requires understanding how objects are composed of parts. Existing benchmarks largely emphasize whole objects, leaving less coverage of the finer concepts, geometric relationships, and physical properties that arise within part-whole hierarchies. This paper introduces PTR, a diagnostic dataset designed to test reasoning at both levels.

PTR contains approximately 80,000 synthetic RGBD images, providing color and depth information, paired with 800,000 machine-generated questions. Its ground-truth annotations describe objects and their parts through semantic instance segmentation, colors, spatial and geometric relationships, and selected physical properties such as stability. The questions use this richer structure to probe several kinds of visual reasoning.

The authors evaluate several leading visual reasoning models and observe many unexpected errors on situations people can readily interpret. These findings expose gaps that object-centered evaluations may leave less visible. The publicly available dataset and baseline models provide a shared testbed for investigating whether systems can connect fine-grained visual structure with conceptual, relational, and physical reasoning.
neurips-2021-ptr-a-benchmark-for-part-ba.tldr: PTR tests reasoning about objects and their parts, revealing substantial mistakes by evaluated visual reasoning models.

paragraphs: Optimizing an uncertain black-box objective can require balancing strong average outcomes against variability. Standard Bayesian optimization targets the expected value, but this paper also considers noise variance that changes with the input. Both the expected objective and its variance are assumed unknown before optimization begins.

The proposed algorithm, RAHBO, seeks a solution with high return and low noise variance while learning the noise distribution during the search. It models the expectation and variance as unknown functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. A risk-aware acquisition function then guides which inputs to evaluate, making variability part of the search criterion.

The authors establish a regret bound and provide a robust rule for reporting a final decision when an application requires one selected solution. Experiments on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter tuning demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. The work connects risk-sensitive search with final selection, so that the concern for variable outcomes is reflected in both stages of the optimization process.
neurips-2021-risk-averse-heteroscedastic.tldr: RAHBO learns unknown input-dependent noise while optimizing a trade-off between high expected return and low variance.

paragraphs: Transferring learned policies can reduce the data needed for a new reinforcement learning task, but transfer also needs to account for risk. This paper considers tasks in a shared domain that differ only in their reward functions. It measures risk through variability in reward streams and develops a way to transfer skills with that variability in view.

The authors extend generalized policy improvement to maximize entropic utilities, allowing improvement to consider both sets of policies and levels of risk aversion. They also extend successor features, which separate environment dynamics from rewards, to represent return variance. The resulting risk-aware successor features preserve the task-generalization advantages of that representation while incorporating risk into decisions.

Experiments use a discrete navigation environment and control of a simulated robotic arm. When the risk of learned policies is taken into account, the proposed method can outperform alternatives, including ordinary successor features. These results support risk-aware reuse of skills within the stated shared-domain, reward-changing task setting.
neurips-2021-risk-aware-transfer-in-rein.tldr: Risk-aware successor features transfer policies across reward-changing tasks while accounting for return variance and different levels of risk aversion.

paragraphs: Efficient attention methods often approximate an attention matrix through sparsity or low rank. This paper observes that the two approaches work best in different regimes governed by attention's softmax temperature. Combining them can improve approximation quality, motivating a method that brings both structures into one attention mechanism.

Scatterbrain combines sparse attention through locality-sensitive hashing with low-rank attention through a kernel feature map. Its design draws inspiration from robust principal component analysis, which separates sparse and low-rank structure. The authors establish that the resulting estimate is unbiased and has provably low error, providing theoretical support for the combined approximation.

Experiments report 2.1 times lower approximation error than baselines when replacing attention in BigGAN and pretrained T2T-ViT. In the latter, attention memory drops by 98% with a reported 1% accuracy decline and no fine-tuning. End-to-end training also yields up to four points better perplexity and five points better average accuracy than sparse or low-rank efficient transformers on the evaluated language and long-range tasks.
neurips-2021-scatterbrain-unifying-spars.tldr: Scatterbrain combines sparse and low-rank attention to improve approximation quality and efficiency across evaluated vision and sequence tasks.

paragraphs: A Trojan attack manipulates training samples so that a neural network acquires behavior an attacker can exploit later. This paper investigates whether such manipulation leaves detectable structural traces inside the trained model. Guided by neuroscientific principles, the authors identify subtle differences that characterize the Trojaned networks they analyze.

Their analysis uses topological tools to represent higher-order dependencies, compare networks robustly, and locate structural abnormalities. One notable observation is the development of shortcuts between shallow and deep layers in Trojaned models. This gives the detection approach a concrete structural motivation: maliciously altered training can be associated with changes in how dependencies connect different network depths.

The authors turn these observations into a strategy for detecting Trojaned models. Across multiple benchmarks, it performs better than the standard baselines included in the comparison. The findings support internal network structure as useful evidence for detecting compromised models, with topology providing both a way to compare networks and a means of locating the abnormalities behind the decision.
neurips-2021-topological-detection-of-tr.tldr: Topological analysis detects structural abnormalities in Trojaned networks and motivates a detector that outperforms tested baselines.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers knowledge from labeled source data to a target domain without target labels. This paper studies why that transfer can fail even when source prediction improves and source and target representations appear more similar. A new lower bound on target error complements existing upper-bound analyses.

The bound shows that reducing source error and marginal distribution mismatch is insufficient to guarantee lower target error. The induced labeling functions can become more mismatched, undermining the apparent progress in alignment. Simple constructed distributions illustrate that the same adaptation approach can succeed, fail, or have an equal chance of either outcome.

Motivated by this analysis, the authors develop poisoning attacks that steer adaptation toward representations with large target errors. On benchmark datasets, adding only 10% poisoned data to the source can reduce target accuracy to nearly zero in some cases. These findings expose limitations of the tested methods and support adversarial evaluation as a way to assess robustness to distributions unfavorable for adaptation.
neurips-2021-understanding-the-limits-of.tldr: A target-error lower bound and poisoning experiments show why source accuracy and distribution alignment alone cannot guarantee successful adaptation.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes learn unknown functions while representing uncertainty. Extending them to curved spaces is useful for scientific problems whose domains are manifolds, such as spheres or tori. This paper focuses on vector fields on those spaces, where a prediction must respect the geometry as well as describe uncertainty.

The authors give a general recipe for constructing gauge-independent kernels from scalar-valued Riemannian kernels. These kernels define Gaussian vector fields: vector-valued Gaussian processes that are coherent with the underlying geometry. Gauge independence means the construction does not depend on an arbitrary choice of local reference frame, allowing geometric consistency to be built into the model.

The paper also extends familiar Gaussian process training techniques, including variational inference, to this setting. That step connects the mathematical construction to methods practitioners can use for learning. The contribution makes geometry-respecting vector-field models accessible through standard training machinery, broadening the types of scientific quantities that Gaussian processes can represent with uncertainty.
neurips-2021-vector-valued-gaussian-proc.tldr: Gauge-independent kernels extend Gaussian processes to geometry-consistent vector fields on manifolds while supporting familiar training methods.
